english: Cyril: …does not bring it to the doors of the tent, that soul shall be utterly destroyed from among its people.’ (Leviticus 17:3–4) At that time those who wished to sacrifice were under every necessity to come to the temple and to the holy city itself, and to complete the sacred rites lawfully, with those of the blood of Levi presenting the offerings. You can hear this plainly from God, who says clearly in Deuteronomy: ‘You may not eat in your cities the tithe of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, the firstborn of your cattle and of your sheep, nor any of the vows that you vow, nor your freewill offerings, nor the first fruits of your hands; but you shall eat it only before the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord your God chooses for himself, you and your sons, and your daughter, and your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite and the stranger who is in your cities; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in everything to which you put your hand. Take care that you do not forsake the Levite for as long as he lives on the earth.’ (Deuteronomy 12:17–19) For the Divine is unapproachable, and a sacrifice without a Levite is unacceptable, since the Levites act as mediators, imitating the Mediator between God and humans, that is, Christ (1 Timothy 2:5). And the law showed plainly that the Church is one and the mystery of Christ is one, and that a sacrifice not performed in the Church is unlawful, or rather is to be rejected and cannot please God; I mean that it showed this by laying down that the sacred rites must not be performed outside the holy tent. You will learn from this too how much care was taken over such matters. It was not at all unlikely, indeed it was the case, that the cities throughout the whole of Judea, which were not easily counted, were separated from Jerusalem by the great distances lying between. And what hardship and toil followed from this? That those who wished to offer first fruits of grain, and of oil and wine as well, had to be able to carry them over so long a road. The labor involved might perhaps have made some reluctant. Yet it was unseemly, indeed utterly out of place, that because the thing was hard and not easy to accomplish for those who lived farther away, the beauty of the truth should be impaired, with the Israelites not bringing their offerings to the holy tent. So, in order that every obstacle in the way might be usefully removed for us, and that the law on this matter might from then on be carried out as the lawgiver intended, Moses gives instruction and sets out the divine will in Deuteronomy, saying: ‘You shall set apart a tenth of all the produce of your seed, the produce of your field, year by year, and you shall eat it before the Lord your God in the place which the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon. There you shall bring the tithes of your grain, of your wine and of your oil, and the firstborn of your cattle and of your sheep, so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God at all times. But if the road is too long for you, and you are not able to carry them up… (Deuteronomy 14:22–24)
translator_notes: The wording matches Lev 17:3–4 (calf/sheep slain in the camp, not brought to the door of the tent, that soul destroyed from its people); Lev 17:8–9 has the same penalty clause but concerns burnt offerings by anyone of Israel or the proselytes, so 17:3–4 is preferred. Deut 12:17–19: ὁμολογίαι rendered 'freewill offerings' (the LXX term for Hebrew nedabot in this verse). The source reads ζῇ ('he lives'); the LXX reads ζῇς ('you live'); I follow the printed text ('all the time that he lives on the earth') and flag it as a probable slip for ζῇς. The 'Mediator between God and humans' (μεσίτης Θεοῦ καὶ ἀνθρώπων) is a clear echo of 1 Timothy 2:5 and is cited. ἐκκλησίᾳ in 'not performed in the Church' is lower-case in Migne but carries the same sense as the preceding Ἐκκλησία; rendered 'the Church' both times. 'And what hard and toilsome thing followed from this?' keeps Cyril's question form (καὶ τί τὸ ἐντεῦθεν σκληρὸν καὶ δυσήνυτον). In 14:23 the printed punctuation joins ἐκεῖ to οἴσεις ('There you shall bring'); followed.

title: Tithes exchanged for silver; the priest as judge, a type of Christ
english: Cyril: …because the place which the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon there is far from you, because the Lord your God will bless you, then you shall sell them for silver, and take the silver in your hands, and go to the place which the Lord your God chooses for his name to be called upon there. And you shall spend the silver on whatever your soul desires, on oxen or on sheep, on wine or on strong drink, or on whatever your soul desires; and you shall eat there before the Lord your God, and you shall rejoice, you and your household, and the Levite who is in your cities, because he has no portion or inheritance with you.’ (Deuteronomy 14:22–27) Do you see the skill of the law? It levels the steep climb, makes rough roads quite passable, and eases even what is very hard. And this, I think, is what was said through the voice of the prophet: ‘The way of the godly has become straight, and the way of the godly is made ready.’ (Isaiah 26:7) Notice too that the Levite is brought in everywhere and of necessity, since the law shows us plainly that the God of all would not accept a sacrifice offered by an unconsecrated hand, in a way that is at odds with the law.
Palladius: So the Levitical order has been held in the highest honor.

Cyril: Entirely so, Palladius. For the priest is a type and an imprint of Christ. Emmanuel has been named the Mediator between God and humans (1 Timothy 2:5), and the Apostle and High Priest of our confession, according to the Scriptures (Hebrews 3:1); he entered once for all into the Holy of Holies, not through the blood of goats and calves but through his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption (Hebrews 9:12). And by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified, according to the Scriptures (Hebrews 10:14). Now look, if you will, at another way as well in which the priest is crowned with the glory of Christ. Christ himself has cried out to us plainly, saying: ‘For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.’ (John 5:22–23) Again, this saying, spoken through the voice of a saint, stands in the sacred writings: ‘There is one Lawgiver and Judge.’ (James 4:12) And the inspired David also sings that ‘God is Judge.’ (Psalm 50:6; Psalm 75:7) Assigning this splendid dignity of judging to those of priestly blood, the lawgiver speaks in this way in Deuteronomy: ‘If a matter for judgment is too hard for you, between one kind of bloodshed and another, between one lawsuit and another, between one injury and another, between one dispute and another, matters for judgment in your cities, then you shall rise and go up to the place which the Lord your God chooses, and you shall come to the priests, the Levites, and to the judge who is in office in those days; and they shall search the matter out and declare the judgment to you. And you shall act according to the matter which they declare to you from the place which the Lord your God chooses, and you shall take care to do all that is laid down for you. You shall act according to the law and according to the judgment that they tell you. You shall not turn aside from the word that they declare to you, to the right or to the left. And the man who acts… (Deuteronomy 17:8–12)
notes_covered: Christ the Mediator and High Priest
translator_notes: ἀποδώσῃ αὐτὰ ἀργυρίου ('give them back for silver') rendered 'sell them for silver'; δώσεις ἀργύριον ἐπί rendered 'spend the silver on'. Isaiah 26:7 matches the LXX word for word (ὁδὸς εὐσεβῶν εὐθεῖα ἐγένετο, καὶ παρεσκευασμένη ἡ ὁδὸς τῶν εὐσεβῶν). 'In a way that is at odds with the law': ἀπᾴδοντος τοῦ νόμου does not agree in gender with χειρός; I take it loosely with the offering or the offerer ('out of tune with the law'), not as a genitive absolute ('the law disagreeing'). Hebrews 9:12 reads εἰς τὰ ἅγια; Cyril has εἰς τὰ Ἅγια τῶν ἁγίων, rendered 'the Holy of Holies' as he wrote it. 'Through the voice of a saint' (δι' ἁγίου φωνῆς) introduces James 4:12 without naming James. 'God is Judge' (Θεὸς κριτής ἐστι): the exact phrase ὅτι ὁ θεὸς κριτής ἐστιν occurs in LXX Psalm 49:6 (English Psalm 50:6) and LXX Psalm 74:8 (English Psalm 75:7); both are cited because the words fit either. The long Greek period (genitive absolutes for Christ, James and David, then 'the lawgiver… says') is broken into several English sentences; the lawgiver here may be God or Moses speaking for God, so it is left lower-case outside the James quotation. The printed text truncates 'the place which the Lord your God chooses ἐκεῖ' (the LXX adds ἐπικληθῆναι τὸ ὄνομα αὐτοῦ); ἐκεῖ is left untranslated. 'The judge who is in office in those days': 'in office' renders ὃς ἂν γένηται ('who may be'). τὸ ἐπὶ τῷδε λαμπρὸν ἀξίωμα rendered 'this splendid dignity of judging', since τῷδε points back to the judging just described. ὧδέ πη rendered 'in this way' (not 'something like this'), because the quotation is exact. αἷμα αἵματος / κρίσις κρίσεως / ἁφὴ ἁφῆς rendered 'one kind of bloodshed / lawsuit / injury and another'; 'stroke' dropped as misleading in modern English.

title: Obey the priest who expounds the law; the lamp set on the lampstand
english: Cyril: …in arrogance, so as not to obey the priest who stands to minister in the name of the Lord your God, or the judge who is in office in those days, that man shall die, and you shall remove the wicked person from Israel. And all the people, when they hear, will be afraid, and will no longer act impiously.’ (Deuteronomy 17:8–13) You see how the law clearly charges those who have chosen to bring a complaint on any ground to make the priest their judge and arbiter. Indeed, ‘you shall take great care to act in keeping with all that is laid down for you’ (Deuteronomy 17:10). For ‘the lips of a priest will guard judgment, and they will seek the law from his mouth,’ as the prophet says (Malachi 2:7). He does not make law himself at all; rather, he conveys faithfully what the lawgiver has decided, setting it out without partiality, and, as the best arbiter of justice, he weighs the judgment in each case with precision. For this reason a charge of savagery and contempt follows those who choose to disobey, and the worst of all evils, that is, death, is appointed for them. For whoever disregards the priest who stands to minister in the name of the Lord God, it says, shall die (Deuteronomy 17:12). Great, then, and truly wonderful is this attendance and ministry under God. Whoever dishonors God’s minister will be subject to judgment and punishment, and whoever spurns the divine dignity will render a bitter account for his contempt. We shall find that our Lord Jesus Christ himself was also concerned for the respect due to this law. For he addressed the crowds of the Jews in this way: ‘The scribes and the Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat; so do all that they tell you, but do not do as they do.’ (Matthew 23:2–3) So let no one judge the priest, even if he is seen to be somewhat slack, and even if he is careless about choosing to live in keeping with the law; but when he interprets the law, let everyone give him ready obedience. For his weaknesses arise from his own will, but what he expounds belongs to God. The things of God, then, must not be dishonored because of what is human.
Palladius: Certainly not.

Cyril: You will learn from this too that the priesthood is a splendid thing, and truly one on which all eyes are fixed. Its beginning is most conspicuous, and so too is its close. For no one could pass unnoticed when he is brought to priestly service, nor again when he is called by God to the dwellings above in heaven and hands the priesthood on to another. That is why Christ too said that those who serve as priests in proclaiming the gospel to the nations (Romans 15:16), and to those of Israel besides, would be conspicuous in every way and without fail, and would receive a glory on which all eyes are fixed. ‘For no one, after lighting a lamp, puts it in a hidden place, nor even under a bed,’ he says, ‘or under a basket, but on the lampstand, so that all who come in may see the light.’ (Luke 11:33; Luke 8:16) That this was truly said, I mean that the divine minister will be in a glory that is conspicuous and admired, let the inspired Isaiah also convince you, when he cries out:
notes_covered: obedience to the priest who teaches the law
translator_notes: 'You shall take great care to act…' (φυλάξῃ σφόδρα ποιῆσαι κατὰ πάντα ὅσα ἂν νομοθετηθῇ σοι) is Cyril's re-quotation of Deuteronomy 17:10 LXX (which has φυλάξῃ σφόδρα ποιῆσαι); set as a quotation and cited. Malachi 2:7 LXX reads χείλη ἱερέως φυλάξεται γνῶσιν ('knowledge'); Cyril's text has κρίσιν ('judgment'), which suits his argument about the priest as judge; translated as he quotes it. 'For whoever disregards the priest… shall die' is a paraphrase of Deuteronomy 17:12, cited without quotation marks. ἀποκομίζει εἰς τὸ εὐθύ rendered 'conveys faithfully' ('carries back straight'). γραφή taken in its legal sense, 'a charge' (indictment). In 'nor again when he is called by God to the dwellings above', ἤγουν (usually 'that is') must here mark the second member (the 'close') against the first (the 'entry'), so it is rendered 'nor again'; μοναί may echo John 14:2 but the allusion is faint and left uncited. 'Those who serve as priests in proclaiming the gospel to the nations' (τὸ εὐαγγελικὸν τοῖς ἔθνεσιν ἱερουργοῦντας κήρυγμα) is a clear verbal echo of Romans 15:16 (ἱερουργοῦντα τὸ εὐαγγέλιον… εἰς τὰ ἔθνη) and is cited. The lamp saying conflates Luke 11:33 (εἰς κρύπτην… οὐδὲ ὑπὸ τὸν μόδιον… ἵνα οἱ εἰσπορευόμενοι… βλέπωσιν) and Luke 8:16 (ὑποκάτω κλίνης… βλέπωσιν τὸ φῶς); ἤγουν ὑπὸ μόδιον ('or rather under a bushel') stands inside the quotation, rendered 'or under a basket'. Matthew 5:15 is close but lacks the 'bed' and 'those who come in'. ἀλλὰ φυλάξῃ σφόδρα… — ἀλλά is Cyril's connective, not part of Deuteronomy 17:10 LXX, so it stands outside the quotation as 'Indeed'. τὸν πονηρόν rendered 'the wicked person' (not 'the evil one', which English readers hear as Satan). πάσχει μὲν γὰρ τὰ ἀπὸ γνώμης οἰκείας rendered 'his weaknesses arise from his own will': πάσχει here refers back to the slackness (παρειμένος, τὸ ῥᾴθυμον) just named, so the sense is his own failings; a more literal 'what he undergoes' was unclear. τῇ περιφανεῖ καὶ τεθαυμασμένῃ agrees with δόξῃ, so 'a glory that is conspicuous and admired'.

title: Aaron dies on the mountain and Eleazar takes up the priesthood
english: Cyril: …‘Go up on a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion.’ (Isaiah 40:9)
Palladius: Anyone can see that this is so. But tell me how the type of this was also foreshadowed for us in the sacred words.

Cyril: Indeed, my friend, you can see the matter quite effortlessly, written out as it were in still coarser types. For God spoke thus to the most holy Moses in Numbers: ‘Take Aaron and Eleazar his son, and bring them up to Mount Hor before the whole congregation; and strip Aaron of his robe, and put it on Eleazar his son; and let Aaron be gathered, and die there. And Moses did as the Lord commanded him, and he brought them up to Mount Hor before the whole congregation; and he stripped Aaron of his garments and put them on Eleazar his son, and Aaron died on the top of the mountain.’ (Numbers 20:25–28) Do you understand, then, how they are brought up: Aaron to die and come to his end, and the one born of him, that is, Eleazar, to take up the priesthood? The mountain would signify what is visible from every side and set on high, what stands out in glory. So let it be said from now on to everyone who is brought to priestly service: ‘A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden.’ (Matthew 5:14)
translator_notes: Isaiah 40:9 matches the LXX (ἐπ' ὄρος ὑψηλὸν ἀνάβηθι, ὁ εὐαγγελιζόμενος Σιων). ἐν παχυτέροις ἔτι τύποις rendered 'in still coarser types' (more material, less refined figures). Numbers 20:25–28 LXX: προστεθείς ('being added') is the LXX rendering of Hebrew 'be gathered [to his people]'; rendered 'let Aaron be gathered' without supplying 'to his people', which is absent from the Greek. The printed text has ἀνεβίβασεν αὐτούς ('brought them up') in 20:27 where the LXX has αὐτόν; followed. συναγωγή rendered 'congregation' as elsewhere in Book 13. 'How they are brought up' renders the single verb ἀναβιβάζεται, which governs both Aaron (to die) and Eleazar (to take hold of the priesthood). Matthew 5:14 matches word for word (οὐ δύναται πόλις κρυβῆναι ἐπάνω ὄρους κειμένη). σκιαγραφέω rendered 'foreshadowed' (sketched in shadow outline); ἀντέχομαι τῆς ἱερωσύνης rendered 'take up the priesthood'.
